content.p: Between 1894 and 1896, Ottoman troops, police and armed Kurdish tribesmen attacked Armenian villages, towns and city quarters across the eastern provinces of the empire. Britannica describes them as a series of atrocities carried out by Ottoman forces and Kurdish irregulars between 1894 and 1896. Historians call them the Hamidian massacres, after Sultan Abdülhamid II, under whose government they took place. The name separates them from the far larger destruction of 1915 and after, which historians now call the Armenian genocide.

The death toll is the most disputed part of the story. The Armenian National Institute gives a range of 100,000 to 300,000 dead. Facing History and Ourselves puts the dead at about 200,000 and says tens of thousands were uprooted between 1894 and 1897. A timeline published by genocide1915.org puts the number killed in 1896 alone at about 150,000. Each figure below is given with the source that made it.
content.h2: A decade of pressure before the killings
content.p: The sultan's government had watched the rise of Armenian political parties with alarm. Britannica names two of them, the Hunchaks and the Dashnaks, founded in 1887 and 1890. Britannica adds that neither party had wide support among Armenians, but that their activity worried Abdülhamid, who was intent on suppressing separatist feeling in the empire. Ottoman officials raised taxes on Armenian villages and, in Britannica's account, stirred up resentment against Armenians among their Kurdish neighbours.

AGBU describes a further step. In 1891 the sultan created the Hamidiye, a Kurdish militia whose leaders were tied directly to the palace. AGBU reports that 65 commanders oversaw some 60,000 men. Those commanders, it argues, became new regional powers, and they used their position to dispossess Armenians. The campaign of dispossession drove families off their land and into cities or abroad, and it was in defence of villagers who had been robbed, abducted and killed that Armenian revolutionary activity grew.

Facing History and Ourselves, citing the American historian Peter Balakian, describes how the government answered Armenian petitions in the early 1890s. In 1890 a gathering of about 200 Armenians in Erzurum was broken up, and more than a dozen people died. A month later a demonstration in Constantinople ended in fighting with police and soldiers. In 1893 Hunchak cells put placards on walls in towns across Anatolia, addressed to Muslims, asking them to stand up against the sultan. Facing History says the placards brought a wave of arrests and torture rather than a revolt.

The first large killings came in the mountain district of Sasun in the summer of 1894. Most pages name a dispute over taxes as the trigger. The Armenian National Institute instead says the government used Armenian resistance to Kurdish encroachment as its excuse. Facing History says the Hunchak party in Sasun urged villagers to withhold payment, and that Ottoman troops were sent to stop the protest. AGBU describes villagers who were made to pay both the state and the Kurdish tribal chiefs, and who refused to pay the second demand. The campaign that followed, in AGBU's words, ravaged nearly 100 villages and killed 7,000 Armenians, with regular troops and Hamidiye regiments under Zeki Pasha taking part.

genocide1915.org gives a different figure for the same events. Its timeline says Kurds attacked the village, the Armenians fought back, and the Kurds then asked Constantinople for help. A force led by General Zeki Pasha joined the Kurds, occupied Sasun and began a mass slaughter in August 1894. It puts the number of Armenians killed at 3,500, and says they died defending their homes and families. The sources do not settle whether the Hamidiye took part in the killing at Sasun.

EBSCO says the Sasun killings were followed by a series of massacres that spread to other parts of Turkish Armenia. The Armenian National Institute says that a series of massacres, beginning in Trebizond on the Black Sea, spread south through nearly every major Armenian-inhabited town in the empire.

In the autumn of 1895 the violence reached the capital. Armenian organisations had planned a demonstration to press the government on reforms that the European powers had demanded, and the sources agree that the protest ended in bloodshed. They differ on the details.

EBSCO says that members of the Hunchak committee in Constantinople organised a demonstration of about 4,000 people, which was meant to move from the cathedral at Kumkapi to the Sublime Porte, the seat of government. EBSCO says Major Servet Bey, aide-de-camp to the minister of police, insulted a student who challenged his authority, and that an Armenian then shot the major dead. Soldiers and police then attacked the marchers. EBSCO puts the number killed at forty, with hundreds wounded, and says that in another part of the city Kurds hunted down Armenians while police and soldiers watched or joined in. EBSCO adds that churches where thousands had sought refuge were set on fire.

AGBU gives a different account. It describes a peaceful protest of 4,000 people held in front of the seat of government, and says police fired into the crowd, causing about 1,000 deaths. It adds that a hunt for Armenians followed in all the neighbourhoods of the city, and that over three weeks most of the city's 160,000 Armenians took refuge in churches. Facing History dates a march of 2,000 Armenians to the Sublime Porte to 1 October 1895, to deliver a petition demanding fair taxation, equality before the law and an end to torture. In its account the protesters were attacked, a police official was killed, and the city saw a week of massacres. The three sources give different dates, numbers and causes for the protest, and each version is reported with its source.

The French ambassador, Paul Cambon, quoted in AGBU, wrote that it was the first time since the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 that Ottoman Christians had resisted Turkish troops. He reported that religious students and clerics joined the police in hunting Armenians, and that prisoners were killed in the courtyard of the police headquarters. British and French diplomats then intervened to end the standoff in the churches. On 6 October 1895 the ambassadors of six European powers demanded reforms from the Ottoman government.

The killings did not stop in the capital. Britannica describes a run of killings in towns with Armenian communities, and the final peak came in December 1895, when about 3,000 people who had sought shelter in Urfa's cathedral were burned to death. Britannica names the town by its modern name, Şanlıurfa. The genocide1915.org timeline places the same event in the first week of the new year, so it dates the Urfa killings to early January 1896 and gives the death toll as 3,000. The Armenian National Institute calls the burning of the Urfa cathedral the single worst atrocity of those months.

On 17 October 1895, according to AGBU, Sultan Abdülhamid signed a decree to end the violence. The attacks continued. AGBU lists dozens of towns and districts where killings took place from October to December 1895, among them Trebizond, Erzurum, Van, Malatya, Diyarbakir, Mardin, Kharpert, Sivas and Samsun. Its account of the method is the same in each town. Community leaders, teachers and clergy were gathered and killed or jailed. Shops and houses were looted and burned, men were killed first, and women and girls were raped. AGBU adds that survivors converted to Islam, which became the norm in dozens of villages in the province of Diyarbakir.

Trebizond is dated differently in the sources. EBSCO says that on 2 October 1895 two unknown assailants shot Bahri Paşa, the former governor of Van, and the local commandant. Armed men then attacked the Armenian quarter, which at the time had about 7,000 Armenian residents, and EBSCO puts the number of Armenians killed at 920. AGBU dates the Trebizond massacre to two days after the ambassadors' demand of 6 October, which would place it around 8 October. Both dates are given here.

The 1915 Genocide timeline says the killings subsided in 1896 when the major powers could no longer ignore reports from the provinces, while new killings continued in Mush and Kilis. It says that about 2,500 communities were emptied of their inhabitants, and that about 100,000 people fled to the Transcaucasus, the Balkans and the United States. Many of those who stayed were stripped of their property. The Institute also says that thousands were forcibly converted to Islam, and that the plunder ruined countless families.

The last large episode began in Constantinople on 26 August 1896. The timeline on genocide1915.org says that 26 Armenian revolutionaries, members of the Dashnak party, stormed the Ottoman Bank and occupied the building. They sent a message to the European powers saying they would not leave until the sultan promised to address their demands and to let an international judge settle the Armenian question. Otherwise, the message said, they would blow up themselves and the bank on the third day.

The Armenian National Institute says the government answered the seizure with reprisals in which five to six thousand Armenians were killed in three days, within sight of the European embassies. Britannica describes the same episode, saying that the revolutionaries had hoped to draw attention to their cause and that more than 5,000 Armenians were killed by mobs of Muslim Turks in the mayhem that followed. Britannica adds that the killings were apparently coordinated by government troops. AGBU gives no figure for this week. The figures are given as reported, without being combined into one count.

The bank episode is the point at which the sources most often stress the foreign response. EBSCO says that Britain and the other great powers refrained from action, and that the Powers drew up a reform plan, the May reform project, which the sultan stalled and finally rejected. EBSCO also says that no reparation or remedy was ever given to the Armenians. The Armenian National Institute says that the conflicting interests of the European states, together with the German emperor's steady support for the sultan, kept the great powers from restraining him.

Each source gives its own total, and the figures are not comparable because they cover different periods and places. The Armenian National Institute gives 100,000 to 300,000 dead. JusticeInfo.net, which reports the figure for the 1895 and 1896 massacres, gives the same range, 100,000 to 300,000. Facing History says about 200,000 Armenians were killed between 1894 and 1897. AGBU says the campaign caused 200,000 deaths and left 50,000 children orphaned. The Cambridge World History of Genocide chapter gives more than 200,000 deaths for the Hamidian massacres. EBSCO says the sultan is said to have killed more than 100,000. genocide1915.org gives about 150,000 killed in 1896. None of the sources gives a count built from named incidents, and the figures are not added together here.

The Ottoman government's own version was different. Facing History says Ottoman officials worked to keep news of the killings from spreading, and that reports were smuggled out and later collected by an investigation of the British, French and Russian governments. Facing History quotes an Ottoman soldier writing to his family that his unit had killed 1,200 Armenians. The same letter, quoted by Facing History, says that 511 had been wounded. Facing History presents this as one soldier's own account and does not extend it to the whole campaign.

The sources agree that the sultan's government set the policy, and they differ on how directly the sultan ordered each killing. Facing History says the attacks were directed by the sultan and carried out by Ottoman soldiers and local militias, which often consisted of Kurdish tribesmen, and that he persuaded the militias to take part by stressing the religious differences between Muslim Kurds and Christian Armenians. The Cambridge chapter argues that the Hamidian massacres showed premeditation and the role of the central government. An international investigation, according to AGBU, found "a grave negligence on the part of the central government" and the involvement of the sultan in the violence.

Facing History also stresses that ordinary people joined in. It quotes the historian Jelle Verheij, who writes that Muslims in Diyarbakir resented Armenians who, by 1895, were accused of dominating trade and building a clock tower higher than a minaret. Facing History also quotes Ronald Grigor Suny, who says religious tension led some to take part, but that many more joined out of greed, once the government had made the killing and looting of Armenians easy. Where the sources name the people who did the killing, they name Ottoman soldiers, police, Kurdish tribesmen and townspeople.

The sources also differ on the Hamidiye at Sasun. AGBU names Hamidiye regiments alongside regular troops, while genocide1915.org names only the soldiers under Zeki Pasha. The sources do not settle how large a share the Hamidiye had.
content.h2: Afterwards and the debate among historians
content.p: The sources give different end dates. Britannica describes the killings as lasting from 1894 to 1896, while Facing History dates them from 1894 to 1897. AGBU reports dispossession of Armenians continuing into the next decade. The sultan's regime lasted until 1909. The Young Turks seized power in 1908 and, genocide1915.org says the Armenians played an important part in that revolution. In April 1909 the sultan tried a counter-coup, and he was forced to abdicate. Massacres of Armenians in Cilicia followed in the same year, and genocide1915.org says that their cause is uncertain.

Historians still debate how to describe the events. The Cambridge chapter notes that the academic literature on the Hamidian massacres was still in its early stages, and that most historians have treated them as the first phase of the later genocide. A smaller group has argued that they should be studied as separate events, in their own context. JusticeInfo.net, which reports Turkey's position on the later events, notes that Turkey accepts that massacres and deportations took place, but describes them as part of an internal conflict. The Armenian National Institute presents the 1894 to 1896 killings as a precedent. It says the Hamidian massacres showed that the Turkish state could carry out a systematic campaign of murder and plunder and gain immunity from the consequences despite international protest.

The disputes about numbers, dates and the chain of command are not settled by the sources. The most important gap is an incident-by-incident count, which the sources do not supply. The figures above are given as the sources give them, each with its author.
